content: Leukemia, derived from the Greek words leukos meaning white and haima meaning blood, refers to a group of malignancies originating from hematopoietic stem cells. These malignancies arise due to genetic abnormalities that result in the clonal proliferation of these cells. Leukemias are classified based on the type of hematopoietic stem cell involved and the duration of the disease. Leukemia is the most common malignancy in children under the age of 15. Among pediatric cases, Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is the most prevalent, accounting for 77% of childhood leukemia cases. In adults, however, Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is the most common form, representing 30% of all leukemia cases in the United States. The unchecked proliferation and reduced apoptosis of these malignant cells can disrupt normal bone marrow function, ultimately leading to bone marrow failure. The clinical presentation, diagnostic findings, laboratory results, and therapeutic approaches vary depending on the specific type of leukemia. Leukemia must be distinguished from other diseases that present with similar symptoms, such as weight loss, night sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, and palpable lymph nodes. Differential diagnoses include hairy cell leukemia, prolymphocytic leukemia, follicular lymphoma, and mantle cell lymphoma. The overall age-adjusted incidence of leukemia in the United States between 2007 and 2011 was 13 cases per 100,000 individuals. The incidence rates vary by age, gender, and race. For example, the age-adjusted incidence of leukemia was 9 per 100,000 individuals in certain age groups. Data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program of the National Cancer Institute provides detailed insights into the incidence and prevalence of leukemia by demographic factors. Graphs and data from SEER illustrate the age-adjusted prevalence of leukemia by race in 2011, as well as the incidence trends by race between 1975 and 2011. Additionally, survival rates differ significantly based on the type of leukemia. For instance, the 5-year relative survival rates for patients diagnosed between 2004 and 2010 vary depending on the specific leukemia subtype and the age of the patients (<65 years versus ≥65 years).
